text: Tatsuo Miyajima (宮島 達男, Miyajima Tatsuo; January 16, 1957 –) is a Japanese sculptor and installation artist who resides in Moriya, Ibaraki prefecture, Japan. His artistic practice frequently involves digital LED counters and centers on the themes of time and space, particularly within Buddhist philosophy. Born in Edogawa City, Tokyo on January 16, 1957, Miyajima graduated from the Oil Painting course in the Fine Arts department of Tokyo National University of Fine Arts and Music in 1984 and completed his MA at the same institution in 1986. Although he initially trained as a painter and briefly identified as a performance artist, his current work primarily consists of installations and sculptures, which he describes as "performing" on his behalf. His core artistic principles are "Keep Changing, Connect with Everything, Continue Forever." In the 1970s, he practiced performance art, influenced by Joseph Beuys, Allan Krapow, and Christo, viewing these works as "actions for society"; however, his desire to create lasting art—contrasting with the ephemeral nature of performance—led him to shift toward sculpture and installation. Miyajima created his first LED counter in 1988, which has become foundational to his later works. These counters typically display two digits in red or green, counting from 1 to 9, and never reach zero, as Miyajima views zero as a purely Western concept. He has connected various displays into interactive systems he calls 'regions.' On August 9, 1945, an atomic bomb was dropped on Nagasaki, killing tens of thousands and destroying much of the city, but a kaki tree survived with over half its trunk blackened and nearly dead. In 1994, arborist Masayuki Ebinuma began treating the tree and restored it, enabling it to produce seedlings. Ebinuma then distributed these saplings to children visiting Nagasaki as a symbol of peace. After learning about this, Miyajima decided to support Ebinuma artistically. In 1995, at an art exhibition, he displayed the saplings and recruited foster parents, receiving ten applications and selecting the former Ryuhoku Elementary School in Taito-ku, Tokyo as the planting site. This led to the conception of the art project "Revive Time: Kaki Tree Project," which established an executive committee. In 1996, the first planting occurred at the former Ryuhoku Elementary School, with Miyajima conducting a workshop at the ceremony. In his works, the LED counters symbolize the lives of anonymous individuals. Miyajima's first solo exhibitions were "Human Stone" at Gallery Parergon, Tokyo in 1983, and "Time" at Maki Gallery, Tokyo in 1986. More recently, he has exhibited at the Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth (1996), Fondation Cartier pour l'Art Contemporain (1996), San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (1997), Miyanomori Art Museum, Hokkaido (2010), and Ullens Center for Contemporary Art, Beijing (2011). He has also participated in numerous group exhibitions, including the Venice Biennale in 1988 and 1999, the Hiroshima City Museum of Contemporary Art (2008), the Museum of Contemporary Art, Sydney (2012), and the Third Asia-Pacific Triennial of Contemporary Art, Queensland Art Gallery, Brisbane (1999). In 2020, Miyajima's works will be featured in the STARS: Six Contemporary Artists from Japan to the World exhibition in Tokyo, which includes a new work titled "Sea of Time – TOHOKU" and documentary footage of the public helping to set counter speeds.
